Came off of playing Ginga Force and Natsuki Chronicles. This is more of a typical arcade-style bullet-hell shmup, without a directly-presented story, but it has the same inimitable charisma that those games have with its presentation, flowing contiguously from stage to stage as you fight alien crafts and UFOs in the skies and in space. You can see a straight through-line from this to Ginga Force, with the same kind of dynamic 3D presentation and camera.

The basic functionality is similar. You have a focussed shot, a spread shot and a shield that functions like the shields in Ginga Force and Natsuki Chronicles. Bullet visibility is usually fine, but there are definitely occasions where you'll die and not understand what hit you. Particularly, there are issues where the game has ambiguous depth and it isn't clear what is on your plane and what isn't, though the game does attempt to remedy this by displaying the numerical difference in depth between you and the enemy entities. Also, sometimes enemies suddenly spawn very close to the bottom of the screen in a way that seems unfair.

In terms of the general game design, though, the enemies and bullet patterns are great. You have a lot of variety, fun gimmicks, and in particular the strengths of your shot types are very defined & distinct which forces you retain situational awareness while avoiding bullets. The shield is an ingenius variation on the usual bomb, where it can be used as both a genuine tactical move to negate bullets and a "get off me!" panic button like the bomb in typical shmups - but it might deplete faster than you realise and lead you to a quick death. And you need extra awareness since backing off in a panic might back you into a bullet that your frontal shield won't negate, and moving sideways through a dense bullet pattern requires an extra level of foresight.

Overall this game is an easy recommend if you like arcade-style shmups. There's a roughness to it, but if you get past that the actual mechanical and enemy/bullet design is multifaceted & varied to an unusual extent, and it's something you can understand as a casual player without getting into scoring systems or advanced play. This is a real gem.

ESCHATOS is a super solid Shmup that'll take you through a 30 minute journey of 26 Areas, divided into 5 Stages, with a selection of 4 Difficulty Levels, with creative use of camera work, very well paced and challenging gameplay, and a Soundtrack I still haven't gotten tired of as I write this.

  The game has a lot of design elements that make the it an easy entry into what's generally (unfairly) seen as the impenetrable Shmup genre. Chief among them is the Shield mechanic that will let you bail out of tough patterns you're unwilling to dodge, in exchange for some energy. Other such elements are the periodic Blue Flash items, pickups that clear bullets off the screen that come in at a regular interval, but can't be stocked. Extra Lives (Extends) are plentiful, totalling about 10 in a run, they're given for destroying a given number of enemies throughout a run, bridging the gap between playing for Survival and Score. Lastly, enemies spawn in predetermined waves, with the next one only coming after the previous one is gone, this is both the basis of the game's Time Attack mode (which is also a blast) and something that de-emphasizes the fundamentals of target prioritization found in other scrolling Shmups, where not killing an enemy will make incoming enemies way harder to deal with. All of these design elements combined with an Easy mode make ESCHATOS a prime recommendation for someone looking to get into the genre.

  For a bit of my personal experience, I can say the quality time I'd get playing and practicing Original Normal was all the motivation I needed to push through and get my first 1CC, because despite there being some particularly brutal screens, such as the Double Mirrors in Stage 5 or the Space Invaders tribute in Stage 4, the game still felt fair, incredibly rewarding to master, and most importantly, fun. These kinds of experiences remind me that video games aren't supposed to be chores you just finish for the sake finishing, they can instead be these super pure experiences that feel engaging at every step of the way regardless of if you're winning or losing. It's because of ESCHATOS being this wonderful kind of game that gives me this sort of experience, that I plan to keep playing it after writing this review, I'm currently aiming to beat Original Hard, and eventually Hardest.

Bonus: What's your favorite track? Mine's the Stage 4 theme: Stellar Light.

Shmups are an oddity of a genre. A niche genre known for having Dark Souls levels of difficulty and being all about repeatedly failing again and again until you've learned how to dance to the genre's at times maddening tunes. It's one of the oldest genres in gaming, having its roots in the arcades of the 70s. That arcade heritage is where the genre got its obsession with extreme difficulty. 

A genre as fixated on being extremely difficult as shmups to the point that some of the games are described as "dodging a rain of death" or a "bullet hell" can be a little difficult to get into. So where does one start if they wanna give the genre a go? Well, Eschatos is a pretty good place. 

Eschatos is not a very lengthy game. A whole run through the game will take you less than 30 minutes. But there's the beauty in the genre. Even on the easiest difficulty Eschatos will give you a challenge, it even inches into bullet hell territory at times. But you'll get the hang of the dance. And when you do, there's higher difficulties waiting. There's alternate modes waiting. There's online leaderboards to compete with the world. You can dance to Eschatos' tunes again and again and eventually master it. 

It's also quite pretty. Visually, Eschatos looks like it escaped from the Dreamcast. A system that's known for quite clean visuals. There's a great soundtrack and a just cool arranged version of said soundtrack. 

In short, TLDR, ETC: A great gateway drug to the shmup genre.

tl;dr: prob the best arcade-style shmup on steam. if nothing, get it for the banger soundtrack.

[h3]What is this game?[/h3]
This is an arcade-style shoot 'em up originally made for the XBOX 360 by a healthcare company. Yes, really.

[h3]So this is shovelware, right?[/h3]
Nope! This is the real deal, made by devs who really understood the genre. There's influence from old arcade games (Tatsujin/Truxton) as well as more "contemporary" bullet-hell-type games (DDP, etc). Furthermore, this builds on them to create its own unique style that feels really fresh and exciting. It's kinda a cult classic for those in the know.

[h3]Counterpoint: this game [i]looks[/i] like shovelware.[/h3]
I won't fight you that this game's visual presentation is its biggest weak point. Allegedly, this game started as a DirectX graphics pet project before being turned into a commercial release, and uhhhhhh it shows. But let's just put that aside, OK?

[h3]So, what actually [i]makes[/i] a shmup good?[/h3]
Enemy patterns, bullet patterns, the general flow of the game, and the soundtrack being pretty good. Not only does ESCHATOS do the first three very well, but it also has a pretty infamously catchy soundtrack made by the very talented Yosuke Yasui. This may be the reason you're even looking at this game and seeing if you should buy it.

[h3]But you didn't answer my question. Like, what's the draw? How is this different from any of the other old arcade games?[/h3]
You're not thinking on the level you need to. Shmups are like roller coasters or the sweet you've been craving in the back of your fridge: ephemeral, short-lived, but exciting above all else. These games don't need to reinvent the wheel. Being a "good" shmup usually means doing the fundamentals very, very well.

That being said, ESCHATOS is really well-designed and has a unique flavor as far as arcade shmups go. You have three buttons allowing you to switch weapons instantly: one for a forward shot, one for a short-ranged wide shot, and one for a shield (quite a rare occurrence in these types of games, but it's very needed here). Your goal is to kill waves of enemies as fast as you can through 26 "areas" where each section of 4-5 areas has its own midbosses and end boss.

The heart of the game is knowing when to use each attack and where. Your forward facing shot can't deal with flanking enemies, so you need the wide shot... but the wide shot can't deal with enemies directly in front of you too well, so you need the forward shot. And when you have your shield up, you can't use either the forward or wide shot AND it has a limited amount of "health" AND can't protect you from attacks from the side or rear (most dangerous of all). Worst of all, using the shield means you aren't killing enemies, which means you'll get overrun assuming you aren't bashing enemies in with it. This is to all say the balance of the weaponry makes this game shine.

The game keeps you on your toes: the game is very fast-paced, and there are a lot of different enemy patterns. All of them will require you to memorize where they come from, their attacks, and which attack(s) best deal with them. Not to mention the bosses, which all have a large amount of attacks including screen-filling lasers that eat through your shield, homing beams, spread attacks you'll have to narrowly dodge through, and if all else fails, ramming into you directly. tl;dr: not a dull moment in this game.

[h3]What if I'm not good at these types of games? Is this just for the "git gud" crowd?[/h3]
ESCHATOS is very ahead of the curve: there's an easy mode that is, if you can believe it, [i]actually easy[/i]. Not only is it very good for learning the game and getting introduced to all the patterns, it's also great if you just want to see the game without needing to be too terribly cracked. Also, the game unlocks infinite credits after playing it enough so don't worry about being locked out of seeing the entire game.

[h3]So is this game worth my hard-earned $15?[/h3]
Yes, and it even goes on sale regularly.

I don't understand how Eschatos receives high praise and I've played a lot of shmups, including Qute's Judgement Silversword. It's not a terrible game, but there's a few issues that make this game annoying.

Scoring in this game is honestly frustrating. You have a score multiplier that goes up after successfully defeating a few waves. Every death and enemy missed drops the multiplier by 1. Dying once, especially towards the end of the stage, can easily drop your multiplier due to popcorn enemies escaping the screen. I don't normally care about scoring, except that higher scores can unlock features such as credits and a stage select sooner than usual.

While I agree the graphics and backgrounds are amazing (stage 4 has a lot of pretty backgrounds), playing the game with the visuals feels like a mess. I struggle a lot with colors, so a lot of the bullets and projectiles blend right in with the background. While some of the camera angles look fantastic, they're aboslutely a mess to deal with. Stage 3 has a bunch of spots where it's hard to judge what can kill you and how far away you really are. 

The one saving grace is the soundtrack. Yousuke Yasui does a wonderful job communicating the sense of urgency throughout the game. I just wish I enjoyed the game as much as I enjoyed the OST.

Eschatos is a relatively simple shoot 'em up from Qute.  There really aren't power or that many weapons systems to keep track of.  However, the game an insane amount of enemies at the player as the camera dramatically twists and winds about further adding to the furious game play.

The player's ship has two attacks.  The first in a powerful forward shot the width of the players ship.  This weapon is better for stronger and/or further away enemies,  The second is a weaker, short range shot with a gap in the front just big enough that missiles can slip though that has a massive spread that works well at dispatching popcorn enemies and chipping at more powerful enemies when the ship can't get directly under them.  

The third system the player's ship has is a forward shield.  This becomes just at important the weapons, as sooner-or-later the enemy shot density just isn't something that can be dodged.  However, using the shield prevent shooting and can't be used for very long before it drains all it power.  To also help with the sheer amount of shots heading toward the player, there's a bullet canceling minor screen wide damage pick-up, but it oscillates back-and-forth so quickly it can be tough to get to when it's really needed.  The player can also toggle through their speed.

The player has to carefully and quickly judge with system is best at any given second in addition to the usual routing of shmups.  This provides a very good challenge and fun experience.  The camera constantly changing may be polarizing to many players though.  While Eschatos is a vertical scrolling shooter, some portions go for more of a third person view.  Which may not be everyone's preference.  Combine this with parts where the camera feels like its on a roller-coaster, and I could very easily see this element turning players off from the game.  Though, I like the dizzying switches in angles, personally.

If the camera doesn't bother much then Eschatos is an easy recommend from me.  It doesn't have the story or ship customization of other Qute shooters, but the simplicity of the game does make it my favorite.  I'm not a fan of the shield mechanic as I prefer a more pure bullethell STG.  But I can forgive that because of the amount of huge tally of enemy ships I can bring down with clever positioning and use of the two weapons for more old school style STG.
